scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Panjurli is venerated in Tulu Nadu, spanning coastal Karnataka and Northern Kerala, where its worship has existed for millennia as part of Bhoota Kola spirit traditions predating mainstream Vedic Hinduism.
Rooted in Dravidian folk belief, the deity stems from an agrarian society intimately connected to cycles of the earth.
According to sacred legend, Panjurli began as an orphaned piglet on Mount Kailash adopted by Goddess Parvati.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Panjurli is invoked during annual festivals, Bhoota Kola gatherings, and Theyyam rituals.
The deity symbolizes environmental stewardship, communal protection, fertility, and justice.
Regarded as a mandatory deity in Tuluva families, Panjurli's ritual functions as a venue for communal decision-making and cross-caste participation, maintaining social harmony and settling disputes.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Ceremonies take place during annual festivals and community gatherings in Tulu Nadu and Northern Kerala shrines.
In the Kasaragod Theyyam tradition, the performer's face is painted in the design known as Rudra Minukku.
The deity represents the divine wild boar, and rituals incorporate ceremonial offerings, including chickens offered by devotees.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The mythological lore centers on Goddess Parvati and Lord Shiva, whose actions led to the boar's transformation and exile to Earth.
In regional pantheons, Panjurli is linked with the sister spirit Kallurti daiva and paired with Guliga, who acts as an enforcer of retribution alongside Panjurli's merciful nature.
In coastal Karnataka, the spirit is invoked as a central daiva within Bhoota Kola.

Panjurli is a hereditary spirit-worship ritual belonging to the Dravidian folk tradition of coastal Karnataka and Northern Kerala, classified as a Theyyam ritual dance in Kerala and a core daiva of Bhoota Kola in Tulu Nadu.

images.description:
The word is derived from būta (Tulu for ‘spirit’, ‘deity’; in turn derived from Sanskrit भूत for ‘free elements’, 'which is purified', 'fit', 'proper', ‘true’, 'past', 'creatures'; Anglicized: ‘bhūta’, ‘bhoota’, ‘bootha’) and kōla (Tulu for ‘play, performance, festival’, or 'shape/form').
A bhūta kōlā or nēmā is typically an annual ritual performance where local spirits or deities (bhūtas, daivas)
